danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: »Hun er kommet for at bo hos mig,« sagde fyrstinde Marja. »Greven og grevinden kommer om nogle dage. Grevinden er i en forfærdelig tilstand; men det var nødvendigt for Natasja selv at se en læge. De insisterede på, at hun fulgte med mig.«
»Ja, er der nogen familie, der er fri for sorg nu?« sagde Pierre henvendt til Natasja. »De ved, det skete den dag, vi blev befriet. Jeg så ham. Sikken en dejlig dreng, han var!«
Natasja så på ham, og som svar på hans ord blev hendes øjne større og lyste op.
»Hvad kan man sige eller tænke som trøst?« sagde Pierre. »Intet! Hvorfor måtte sådan en pragtfuld dreng, så fuld af liv, dø?«
»Ja, i disse tider ville det være svært at leve uden tro...« bemærkede fyrstinde Marja.
»Ja, ja, det er virkelig sandt,« afbrød Pierre hende hastigt.
»Hvorfor er det sandt?« spurgte Natasja og så opmærksomt ind i Pierres øjne.
»Hvordan kan du spørge om det?« sagde fyrstinde Marja. »Blot tanken om, hvad der venter...«
Natasja afbrød igen, uden at vente på at fyrstinde Marja blev færdig, og så spørgende på Pierre.
»Og fordi,« fortsatte Pierre, »kun den, der tror, at der er en Gud, som styrer os, kan bære et tab som hendes og... Deres.«
Natasja havde allerede åbnet munden for at tale, men standsede pludselig. Pierre vendte sig hastigt bort fra hende og henvendte sig igen til fyrstinde Marja med spørgsmål om sin vens sidste dage.

Pierres forvirring var nu næsten forsvundet, men samtidig følte han, at hans frihed også helt var borte. Han følte, at der nu var en dommer over hans hvert ord og handling, hvis dom betød mere for ham end hele den øvrige verdens. Mens han talte, overvejede han, hvilket indtryk hans ord ville gøre på Natasja. Han sagde ikke med vilje ting for at behage hende, men hvad end han sagde, betragtede han det fra hendes synsvinkel.

Fyrstinde Marja begyndte — modstræbende som sædvanligt i sådanne tilfælde — at fortælle om den tilstand, hvori hun havde fundet fyrst Andrej. Men Pierres ansigt, der sitrende af bevægelse, hans spørgsmål og hans ivrige, rastløse udtryk tvang hende gradvist til at gå i detaljer, som hun selv frygtede at genkalde.

»Ja, ja, og så...?« blev Pierre ved med at sige, mens han lænede sig mod hende med hele kroppen og ivrigt lyttede. »Ja, ja... så han blev rolig og blødgjort? Med hele sin sjæl havde han altid søgt én ting — at være fuldkommen god — og derfor kunne han ikke frygte døden. De fejl, han havde — om han overhovedet havde nogen — var ikke hans egen skyld. Så han blev blødere?... Sikke en lykkelig ting, at han så Dem igen,« tilføjede han med et pludseligt blik på Natasja med tårefyldte øjne.
Natasjas ansigt sitrede. Hun rynkede brynene og sænkede blikket et øjeblik. Hun tøvede et sekund — om hun skulle tale eller ej.

»Ja, det var lykke,« sagde hun med sin stille stemme med de dybe brysttoner. »For mig var det i hvert fald lykke.« Hun holdt en pause. »Og han... han... han sagde, at han ønskede det netop i det øjeblik, jeg trådte ind i værelset....«
Natasjas stemme brast. Hun rødmede, pressede sine foldede hænder mod knæene og begyndte så med en tydelig kraftanstrengelse at beherske sig, løftede hovedet og begyndte at tale hurtigt.

»Vi vidste intet om det, da vi drog fra Moskva. Jeg turde ikke spørge om ham. Så fortalte Sonja mig pludselig, at han rejste med os. Jeg anede intet og kunne ikke forestille mig, hvilken tilstand han var i, alt hvad jeg ønskede, var at se ham og være hos ham,« sagde hun med bævende stemme og hurtig ånde.
Og uden at lade dem afbryde fortalte hun, hvad hun aldrig før havde nævnt for nogen — alt hvad hun havde gennemlevet i de tre uger af deres rejse og ophold i Jaroslavl.

Pierre lyttede med åben mund og øjne rettet mod hende, fulde af tårer. Mens han lyttede, tænkte han hverken på fyrst Andrej eller på døden eller på det, hun fortalte. Han lyttede til hende og følte kun medlidenhed med hende for den lidelse, hun gennemgik nu, mens hun talte.
Fyrstinde Marja, der anstrengt holdt tårerne tilbage med rynkede bryn, sad ved siden af Natasja og hørte for første gang historien om de sidste dage af sin brors og Natasjas kærlighed.
Det var tydeligt, at Natasja havde brug for at fortælle den smertefulde, men dog glade historie.
Hun talte og blandede de mest ubetydelige detaljer med sjælens inderste hemmeligheder, og det virkede, som om hun aldrig kunne blive færdig. Flere gange gentog hun det samme to gange.
Dessalles' stemme hørtes uden for døren og spurgte, om lille Nikolaj (fyrst Andrejs søn) måtte komme ind og sige godnat.
»Nå, det var det hele — alt sammen,« sagde Natasja.
Hun rejste sig hurtigt, netop som Nikolaj trådte ind, løb næsten hen til den dør, der var skjult bag forhæng, slog hovedet mod den og flygtede ud af rummet med et støn af enten smerte eller sorg.
Pierre stirrede på den dør, hun var forsvundet igennem, og forstod ikke, hvorfor han pludselig følte sig helt alene i verden.
Fyrstinde Marja vækkede ham af hans tankeflugt ved at henlede hans opmærksomhed på sin nevø, der var kommet ind i stuen.

I det øjeblik af følelsesmæssig ømhed berørte den unge Nikolajs ansigt, der lignede hans fars, Pierre så stærkt, at da han havde kysset drengen, rejste han sig hurtigt, tog sit lommetørklæde frem og gik hen til vinduet. Han ville tage afsked med fyrstinde Marja, men hun ville ikke lade ham gå.
»Nej, Natasja og jeg går somme tider ikke i seng før efter to, så lad være med at gå. Jeg bestiller aftensmad. Gå ned, vi kommer straks.«
Inden Pierre forlod rummet, sagde fyrstinde Marja til ham: »Det er første gang, hun har talt om ham på den måde.«

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: "She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a terrible state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They made her come with me."
"Yes, is there a single family untouched by grief right now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and by way of answer her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say or think of as consolation?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did such a splendid boy, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, in these times it would be hard to live without faith..." remarked Princess Mary.
"Yes, yes, that's absolutely true," Pierre quickly agreed.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking intently into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what awaits us—"
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked inquiringly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre continued, "only someone who believes that God is watching over us can bear a loss like hers and... yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to speak but suddenly stopped. Pierre quickly turned away from her and addressed Princess Mary again, asking about his friend's last days.

Pierre's confusion had now almost vanished, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had completely disappeared. He felt there was now a judge of his every word and action whose judgment mattered to him more than the judgment of all the rest of the world. As he spoke he was constantly aware of the impression his words were making on Natasha. He didn't deliberately say things to please her, but whatever he said, he judged himself through her eyes.

Princess Mary—with the reluctance usual in such cases—began describing the state in which she had found Prince Andrew. But Pierre's face, quivering with emotion, his questions and eager, restless expression, gradually compelled her to go into details she shrank from calling up in her own mind.

"Yes, yes, and so...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening intently. "Yes, yes... so he found peace and grew gentle? He had always sought one thing with all his soul—to be completely good—so he couldn't have been afraid of death. His flaws—if he had any—didn't come from within himself. So he did find peace?" Pierre asked. "What a blessing that he saw you again!" he added to Natasha.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated briefly over whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said in her quiet, deep voice. "For me it certainly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he said he was hoping for exactly that at the moment I came to see him..." Her voice broke.
Natasha blushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, and then, with a visible effort to control herself, lifted her head and began speaking rapidly.

"We knew nothing when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be near him," she said, trembling with agitation.
And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell what she had never told anyone—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of their journey and time in Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened with parted lips and eyes brimming with tears. As he listened, he thought not of Prince Andrew or of death, not of what she was telling him. He listened to her and felt nothing but compassion for the suffering she was going through now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning in her effort to hold back tears, sat beside Natasha and heard for the first time the story of those last days of her brother's love and Natasha's.
Clearly, Natasha needed to tell this painful yet somehow joyful story.
She spoke, weaving the most trivial details together with the deepest secrets of her soul, and it seemed she could never finish. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice was heard outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas might come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all—everything," said Natasha.
She jumped up quickly, almost ran to the door hidden behind curtains, bumped her head against it, and rushed from the room with a moan of either pain or grief.
Pierre gazed at the door through which she'd disappeared and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt completely alone in the world.
Princess Mary roused him from his thoughts by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

At that moment of emotional tenderness, young Nicholas's face—so like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy, he quickly stood up, pulled out his handkerchief, and walked to the window. He wanted to say goodbye to Princess Mary, but she would not let him go.
"No, Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought. Go downstairs—we'll be right there."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's spoken about him like that."
